pedagogy.summary:
• Age/Topic — Dinosaurs Around the World (ages 7–9): different dinosaurs lived on different continents, and fossils have been found on EVERY continent — including Antarctica — showing dinosaurs were a global phenomenon; the same kinds of dinosaur found on now-distant continents hint that the land was once joined.
• Standards — UK (DfE): supports KS2 Geography (world continents/maps) and science 'working scientifically'; seeds the Y6/KS3 idea of Earth change (continental movement).
• Standards — US (NGSS): connects to fossil evidence for past life/Earth history (3-LS4-1 into MS-ESS2-3, patterns of fossils and rock across continents as evidence of plate motion).
• Operational details — Two ideas: (1) GLOBAL distribution — map famous finds to places (T. rex in North America, Velociraptor in Mongolia, Argentinosaurus in Argentina, Cryolophosaurus in Antarctica) and note fossils occur on all seven continents. (2) The inference seed — matching dinosaurs (and plants like Glossopteris) on continents now separated by oceans is evidence the continents were once joined (Pangaea/Gondwana) and have since drifted apart. Add the vivid point that Antarctica was once warm and forested. Keep continental drift qualitative ('the land slowly moved') rather than mechanistic. Note Antarctica has the FEWEST finds (ice hides the rocks), a nice 'absence of evidence' nuance.
• Checkpoint — Tier A (~7): says dinosaur fossils are found all over the world, even Antarctica. Tier B (~8): names a dinosaur with where it was found. Tier C (~9): suggests that the same dinosaur on now-separate continents means the land was once joined and has moved apart.
bestPractices: Use a world map as the organising surface — pin finds to places so 'global' is seen, not just stated.
Include Antarctica as the surprising 'capstone' continent (once warm/forested; Cryolophosaurus) to make 'everywhere' vivid.
Introduce the joined-land inference gently: same dinosaur/plant on distant continents → they were once connected and drifted apart.
Add the honest nuance that Antarctica has the fewest finds because ice hides the rock — fewer finds ≠ fewer dinosaurs (absence of evidence).
Link to children's geography knowledge of continents and oceans to anchor the spatial reasoning.
keyRepresentations: A world map with pins: T. rex (N America), Velociraptor (Mongolia), Argentinosaurus (Argentina), Cryolophosaurus (Antarctica).
A Pangaea 'jigsaw' showing today's continents once fitted together, with a shared dinosaur/plant straddling the join.
A 'then vs now' Antarctica: warm forest → ice sheet.
A find-density shading showing Antarctica sparse (ice cover) vs North America/China/Argentina rich.
commonMisconceptions: 'Dinosaurs only lived in a few hot places' — fossils are found on all seven continents, including Antarctica.
'Antarctica never had dinosaurs because it's frozen' — it was once warm and forested; ice now hides most fossils.
'The same dinosaur on two continents means it swam across the ocean' — the continents were joined then and have since drifted apart.
'Fewer fossils in Antarctica means fewer dinosaurs lived there' — it mostly reflects how hard they are to find under ice.
'Continents have always been where they are now' — land masses move slowly over millions of years.

learn.summary: Dinosaurs Around the World (ages 7–9): dinosaur fossils have been found on all seven continents, including Antarctica, showing dinosaurs were a global phenomenon. The same kinds of dinosaur (and plants like Glossopteris) found on continents now separated by oceans hint that the land was once joined (Pangaea/Gondwana) and has slowly drifted apart. Learners map famous finds to places on a world map, meet the surprising Antarctica case, and reassemble the joined landmass to see why the same creature appears on now-distant continents. Keep continental drift qualitative ('the land slowly moved').

activities.title: Map the finds: dinosaurs lived everywhere
feedback: If a learner says dinosaurs only lived in a few hot places, point to pins on multiple continents and ask them to count how many continents are represented — all seven.
If they are surprised by the Antarctica pin, confirm it: a crested meat-eater called Cryolophosaurus lived there.
Reinforce: naming a dinosaur AND its location (e.g. 'Velociraptor in Mongolia') shows the global spread, not just that dinosaurs existed.
activities.rationale: This is fundamentally a 'where' topic; pinning finds to places on a map lets 'global' be seen rather than merely stated, and anchors the spatial reasoning to children's existing knowledge of continents and oceans. Tap-to-reveal interaction (dinosaur name, photo, 'found in ___') can make each discovery concrete, but a printed map with movable labels achieves the same mapping.
sourceClaims: Dinosaur fossils have been found on all seven continents, including Antarctica; the greatest diversity comes from North America, China, and Argentina, while Antarctica has the fewest finds because ice covers most rock.
learnerActions: Work with a world map and place or reveal find-pins for famous dinosaurs, one or more on every continent: T. rex (North America), Argentinosaurus (Argentina, South America), Iguanodon (England and Belgium, Europe), Spinosaurus (Egypt and Morocco, Africa), Velociraptor (Mongolia, Asia), Muttaburrasaurus (Australia) and Cryolophosaurus (Antarctica).
For each pin, say the dinosaur's name and the continent/place it was found in.
Count the continents represented and state out loud that fossils have been found on all seven, including Antarctica.
Use a shading or density layer to notice where most finds come from (North America, China, Argentina) versus the sparse Antarctica.
activities.intendedInsight: Dinosaurs were not a local curiosity confined to a few hot places — they lived across the whole planet, and fossils of them have been found on every continent.

activities.title: The Antarctica surprise: fewer finds is not fewer dinosaurs
feedback: If a learner says Antarctica never had dinosaurs because it's frozen, show the 'then' picture: it was once warm and forested, and Cryolophosaurus is firm evidence dinosaurs lived there.
If they conclude few finds means few dinosaurs, re-ask: what makes fossils hard to find there? (Ice hides the rock.)
activities.rationale: Antarctica is the vivid 'capstone' continent that makes 'everywhere' real and introduces an honest reasoning nuance about how discovery conditions, not past life, drive the number of finds.
sourceClaims: Dinosaur fossils have been found on all seven continents, including Antarctica; the greatest diversity comes from North America, China, and Argentina, while Antarctica has the fewest finds because ice covers most rock.

Matching fossils (e.g. the plant Glossopteris and shared Triassic reptiles) on continents now separated by oceans provided evidence that the land was once joined as Pangaea/Gondwana and has since drifted apart; Antarctica was once warm and forested with dinosaurs such as Cryolophosaurus.
learnerActions: Compare a 'then vs now' picture of Antarctica: once warm and forested → today an ice sheet.
Explain why Antarctica has the fewest dinosaur finds: ice now covers most of the rock, making fossils very hard to find.
Decide whether 'fewer fossils found in Antarctica' means 'fewer dinosaurs lived there', and explain your reasoning.
State that Cryolophosaurus lived in Antarctica back when it was warm and forested.
activities.intendedInsight: Antarctica was once warm and forested and had dinosaurs; the few fossils found there reflect how hard they are to find under ice, not a lack of dinosaurs — an 'absence of evidence is not evidence of absence' nuance.

activities.title: Reassemble the land: why the same dinosaur appears oceans apart
feedback: If a learner says the dinosaur swam or flew across the ocean, introduce the joined land: the continents were once connected, so the animal simply walked across land that later tore apart into an ocean.
If they think continents have always been where they are now, show them sliding back together and note the land moves slowly over millions of years.
Praise answers that use the matching-fossil pattern as the reason, e.g. 'the same plant sits across the join, so the two continents must once have been one piece of land.'
activities.rationale: Physically reassembling the continents so shared-fossil bands align makes the joined-land inference visible and active, directly addressing the 'they swam across' and 'continents are fixed' misconceptions. Drag-to-fit interaction where a correct match reveals 'once joined' can make the mechanism concrete; a paper continent-cutout jigsaw works equally well. Keep drift qualitative ('the land slowly moved'), not mechanistic.
sourceClaims: Matching fossils (e.g. the plant Glossopteris and shared Triassic reptiles) on continents now separated by oceans provided evidence that the land was once joined as Pangaea/Gondwana and has since drifted apart; Antarctica was once warm and forested with dinosaurs such as Cryolophosaurus.
learnerActions: Start from today's continents and slide/drag them back together so they fit like a jigsaw into one giant landmass (Pangaea/Gondwana).
Line up a shared dinosaur or plant (e.g. Glossopteris) so it sits across a seam where two continents once joined.
Explain in your own words how the same kind of dinosaur ended up on two continents now separated by a huge ocean (e.g. Africa and South America).
Contrast two explanations: 'the dinosaur swam across the ocean' versus 'the land was joined then and has since drifted apart' — and say which the fossil pattern supports.
activities.intendedInsight: Matching dinosaurs and plants on now-distant continents are evidence the land was once joined and has slowly drifted apart over millions of years; the dinosaur walked across land that later split, rather than crossing an ocean.

activities.title: Check and explain (matching plus reasoning)
feedback: A full answer explains the global spread AND infers the continents were once joined and later drifted apart, using the matching fossils on now-separated continents as the main evidence (Antarctica's dinosaur fossils can add that the ancient world was very different from today).

A partial answer accepts that dinosaurs lived worldwide but cannot yet explain how the same or closely related kinds of fossils ended up on continents now separated by ocean — return to the reassembly activity.
A gap-level answer keeps continents in today's positions and moves the animals across the water; reteach the joined-land idea with the jigsaw.

Example of a strong explanation: 'Long ago the continents were joined as one big landmass, so the dinosaur walked across land that later split apart; over millions of years the land drifted to where the continents are now, leaving the same fossils on both sides of the ocean.'
activities.rationale: Matching and selecting the correct continent confirm the facts cleanly, but the written/spoken explanation of the Africa–South America case is what discriminates a learner who assumes fixed continents (animals crossed the ocean) from one who understands the land itself moved. Recognition items alone do not elicit this independent reasoning, so an open explanation task is needed.
learnerActions: Match each dinosaur to the continent where it was found (e.g. T. rex → North America, Velociraptor → Asia (found in Mongolia), Argentinosaurus → South America (found in Argentina), Cryolophosaurus → Antarctica).
Answer: which continent, surprisingly, also has dinosaur fossils? (Antarctica.)

Respond to the diagnostic prompt in writing or speech: 'The same kind of dinosaur fossil has been found in both Africa and South America, which today are separated by a huge ocean. How could the same dinosaur have lived on two continents so far apart? Explain your thinking.'

Tackle the deeper prompts: 'Antarctica is frozen today, yet dinosaur fossils are found there — what does that tell you about the past?' and 'If the continents were all joined, why don't we find exactly the same dinosaurs everywhere?'
activities.intendedInsight: Learners can recall the global distribution AND construct an explanation for matching fossils, distinguishing 'the animals crossed the ocean' from 'the land was joined and drifted apart.'

constraints: Keep continental drift qualitative at this age ('the land slowly moved over millions of years'); do not introduce plate-tectonic mechanism.
Matching and single-answer selection confirm recall but do not by themselves show a learner can construct the joined-land inference; include an open explanation task for that.

Tap-to-reveal maps, drag-to-reassemble puzzles, shading layers and a spinnable globe are helpful optional ways to make the mechanism concrete — they are not required; paper maps and continent cutouts can serve the same purpose.
The 'fewest finds in Antarctica' point should be framed as a discovery-conditions effect (ice hides rock), not as proof that fewer dinosaurs lived there.
A reteach prerequisite micro-topic exists for the 'dinosaurs only lived in one part of the world' misconception; establish global spread before tackling how matching species crossed.
reviewNotes: This is an agent semantic rewrite of saved teaching research without fresh source verification; sources were not re-fetched. Activities are research-informed proposals, not validated interventions.

The source cites a Natural History Museum (UK) news URL dated 2026 about a 'first-ever dinosaur fossil discovered on Antarctica (a titanosaur)', which sits in tension with the long-established presence of Cryolophosaurus and other Antarctic dinosaur fossils stated elsewhere in the same row. The claim text and date should be checked; the activities rely only on the well-supported points (fossils on all continents, Cryolophosaurus, Glossopteris matching, drift).

Glossopteris is a seed-fern plant primarily associated with the Permian/early Mesozoic Gondwana flora, and the shared-reptile evidence (e.g. Lystrosaurus) is Triassic; presented here for ages 7–9 simply as 'the same plant/animal on now-distant continents,' which is appropriate at this level but simplifies the timeline.

The non-preferred 3D globe and conversation options from the source were not included as activities: the globe is retained as an optional affordance, and a text-only conversation does not itself present the map-based distribution or the visual reassembly — but this is a narrow fit judgement about observable affordances, not an established claim that dialogue 'cannot teach' the inference.

probeDeeper: Antarctica is frozen today, yet dinosaur fossils are found there. What does that tell you about the past?
How could land that now sits in a cold place once have been joined to a warm continent?
If the continents were all joined, why don't we find exactly the same dinosaurs everywhere?
assess.correctAnswer: Long ago the continents were joined together as one big landmass, so the dinosaur could walk across land that later split apart. Over millions of years the land drifted to where the continents are now, leaving the same fossils on both sides of the ocean.

errorPatterns.pattern: Continents are fixed, so the animals crossed the ocean: 'the dinosaurs swam or flew across.'
errorPatterns.nextMove: Introduce joined continents and slow drift; the land moved, the dinosaurs simply walked across it before it split.
errorPatterns.distractor: The dinosaurs swam across the ocean from one continent to the other.
errorPatterns.revealedBy: Keeps the continents in today's positions and moves the animals across the water to explain the match.

errorPatterns.pattern: Dinosaurs couldn't live in cold places like Antarctica.
errorPatterns.nextMove: Note that Antarctica was warmer and differently placed in the Mesozoic; fossils there are firm evidence dinosaurs lived on every continent.
errorPatterns.revealedBy: Denies that fossils are found in Antarctica, or says it was always too cold there.

errorPatterns.pattern: Dinosaurs only lived in one part of the world.
errorPatterns.nextMove: Show the global spread of discoveries — every continent — before tackling how matching species crossed.
errorPatterns.distractor: That's impossible — dinosaurs only ever lived in one place.
errorPatterns.revealedBy: Treats dinosaurs as local to a single region and calls worldwide finds impossible.

responseLevels.gap: Thinks dinosaurs lived only in certain places and explains matching fossils by the animals swimming or flying across the ocean.
responseLevels.full: Explains the global distribution AND infers the continents were once joined and later drifted apart, using the Antarctica evidence to support the idea.
responseLevels.partial: Accepts that dinosaurs lived worldwide but cannot explain how identical fossils ended up on continents now separated by ocean.

assess.diagnosticPrompt: The same kind of dinosaur fossil has been found in both Africa and South America, which today are separated by a huge ocean. How could the same dinosaur have lived on two continents so far apart? Explain your thinking.
assess.whatMakesItDiscriminate: A child who assumes continents were always where they are now explains it by the animals crossing the ocean. A child who understands says the land itself was joined then and has since drifted apart.
